items.desc: A veteran of the globally connected avant-garde music scene, Hiromi Moritani aka Phew has been active since the late 1970s, when she was the vocalist of Osaka post-punk band Aunt Sally. Going solo in the 1980s, she began a prolific and highly collaborative career, working with Can, Jim O'Rourke, Boredoms, The Raincoats, Ryuichi Sakamoto and numerous other fellow travellers in boundary pushing music. Stylistically, her music features prominent improvisation, and aligns with post-punk, industrial, minimalism, noise and - in later years - electronic compositions. Compiled and mixed by Brian Cone…
items.tags: Post Punk, Experimental, Industrial , Art Rock
items.title: In Focus: Phew

items.desc: American composer and synthesist, Pauline Anna Strom first began releasing music in the early 1980s under the moniker Trans-Millenia Consort. Working for the most part in isolation, she crafted immersive synth soundscapes, conjuring imagined worlds between ancient myth and imagined futures. After her early records fell out of circulation, her work was introduced to new audiences in 2017 through the compilation Trans-Milenia Music. She returned to releasing original work with the 2020 album Angel Tears in Sunlight, released by RVNG Intl just months after her passing.
items.title: In Focus: pauline anna strom

items.desc: Emerging from the creative crucible of LA's loose "beat scene" collective of the mid-2000s alongside fellow artists such as Ras G, Thundercat, and Nosaj Thing, Steven Ellison aka Flying Lotus took a painterly approach to the structure of hip hop production. Part of a jazz and soul lineage that includes Motown songwriter Marilyn McLeod and spiritual jazz matriarch Alice Coltrane, Ellison infused instrumentals with loose improvisational flourishes and an experimental spirit that frequently breaks beyond the definitions of hip hop. His style has expanded further incorporating R&B, jazz, IDM, and…

items.desc: CONTENT WARNING: Racism Doubtless the most influential living American composer, Steve Reich shattered the conventions of the classical music establishment almost by accident. Taking a recording of a San Francisco street preacher, Reich played two reels simultaneously in a round, but soon discovered one machine played slower than the other, creating an endlessly complex series of irrational and rational harmonies between the two tapes. This phasing effect discovered on "It's Gonna Rain", would define Reich's career - transferring the technique into the human realm with repetitious, hypnotic a…
items.title: In Focus: Steve Reich

items.desc: In the mid 1970s, guitarist Kourosh Yaghmaei was the king of Iranian rock music - his records sold in the millions and he was internationally famous among the Iranian diaspora. But in 1979, following the Iranian revolution, his music was heavily censored and banned on the radio by the fundamentalist Iranian regime for it's psychedelic style, a sound considered too "western". Kourosh Yaghmaei's music could have been lost forever to wider audiences, but a relaxing in rules in the 1990s allowed Yaghmaei's music to be released once again. Selected by Lara Sarkissian.
items.title: In Focus: Kourosh Yaghmaei

items.desc: John Martyn, known to his family as Iain David McCready, first rose to prominence in the British folk revival scene of the mid-1960s, alongside artists like Nick Drake and Fairport Convention. "Folk" was a label Martyn always rejected, and his expansive style reflected this – there are touches of Debussy in his compositions, and his echoplex-led sustained notes were famously inspired by jazz artist Pharoah Sanders. It's perhaps ironic that Martyn's music was often so delicate - he was not. A notorious carouser, Martyn drank, and fought, and badly mistreated the women and children in his life.…

Associated with musical genres including Afropop, jazz, and world music, she was an advocate against apartheid and white-minority government in South Africa. Selected and mixed by TrYb.

items.desc: Soon after he first emerged in the mid-’50s, pianist Cecil Taylor was the most advanced improviser in jazz; five decades later he is still the most radical. Although in his early days he used some standards as vehicles for improvisation, since the early ’60s Taylor has stuck exclusively to originals. To simplify describing his style, one could say that Taylor’s intense atonal percussive approach involves playing the piano as if it were a set of drums.
